The selected source, **"Scoping-and-Defining-an-Enterprise-Data-Platform-DeepResearch.md"**, outlines how to define project boundaries to prevent scope creep, but it treats these tools as integrated components of the requirements-gathering process rather than standalone procurement or legal contracts. 

Here is how these artifacts are structured and positioned within standard requirements deliverables according to your selected source, followed by the specific gaps on contract-level protection that the source does not cover.

---

### 1. Scope Exclusion List (Out-of-Scope Items)
The source identifies defining what is "out-of-scope" as a fundamental requirement of the scoping phase, embedding it directly into the core requirements documentation:
*   **Within the BRD:** A dedicated "project scope" section is one of the seven non-negotiable components of every Business Requirements Document (BRD) [1]. The source emphasizes that **"business requirements should be numbered, testable statements each tied to an objective, with explicit scope exclusions"** [1]. This ensures a clear, structured boundary for what the platform will and will not deliver.
*   **Within the PRD:** For product-centric or agile methodologies, a Product Requirements Document (PRD) must explicitly catalog **"out-of-scope items"** alongside risks and open questions [2] to protect the product team and vendors from post-signature creep.

### 2. Assumption Log and Client Dependency Register
Rather than managing these as isolated registers, standard requirements engineering frameworks integrate assumptions and dependencies directly into system specifications to bound technical liability:
*   **Requirements Integration:** The source notes that **"many teams add assumptions"** directly into the BRD to outline the environmental context of the requirements [1].
*   **IEEE 830 / SRS Standard:** Under the IEEE 830 standard for a Software Requirements Specification (SRS) or Functional Requirements Specification (FRS), the "overall description" section must explicitly document **"constraints, assumptions/dependencies"** [2].
*   **Cross-Team Dependencies:** Within a PRD, the standard is to formally catalog **"open questions, risks, and cross-team dependencies"** [2]. This establishes clear hand-offs and boundaries between what the platform development team must build and what external teams must provide.

---

### Gaps in the Selected Source Regarding Procurement
While your selected source establishes assumptions, dependencies, and exclusions as critical sections within the requirements hierarchy (BRD, FRS, PRD) to define system boundaries [1, 2], **it does not cover procurement-specific contract drafting, legal liability clauses, or dedicated, standalone registers designed for commercial vendor negotiations.** 

---

### Source-Grounded Best Practices to Prevent Scope Creep & Failure
To protect a fixed-price contract and prevent costly failures, the selected source recommends several rigorous practices that go beyond simply listing assumptions:

*   **Rigorous Change Impact Analysis via the RTM:** To manage change requests objectively and prevent scope creep, you must maintain a **Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)** [3]. The RTM maps every business requirement back to its strategic objective and forward to its physical design components (e.g., specific columns in a Source-to-Target Mapping) and verification test cases [3]. When a change is proposed, the RTM allows you to perform an automated **"impact analysis"** to see exactly what downstream artifacts must change, providing the objective data needed to justify contract adjustments [3].
*   **Treat Data-Specific Deliverables as Non-Negotiable:** The source warns that data platform projects do not fail due to generic software requirements gaps; they fail because they omit data-specific artifacts [4, 5]. To bound vendor liability and prevent "data swamps," the requirements package must include a technical **Data Dictionary** [6], a version-controlled **Source-to-Target Mapping (STM)** [7], **Data Quality (DQ) Requirements** mapped to the DAMA canonical six dimensions [8], and design-time **Data Lineage Documentation** [9]. Leaving data quality unmanaged is a massive risk; poor data quality costs organizations an average of **\$12.9 million annually** [4].
*   **Strict Sequential Governance:** To prevent the build team from having to rediscover requirements, the work must follow a strict sequential order: **(1) Business Case, (2) Governance Charter and stewardship definitions (completed in parallel to establish rules), (3) BRD, (4) FRS/PRD + NFRs, (5) Data-specific artifacts, and (6) User stories** [5]. No downstream phase should begin until its upstream anchor is formally signed off [5].
